Recent work supports adaptive interest evolution, but these searches did not establish a 2024–2026 GRU4Rec method specifically validating learned boundary-triggered resets. [IMA/EMA (2024)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10400839/) detects new intents, retains existing intents and removes inactive ones under memory constraints; this concerns incremental intent adaptation rather than recurrent state resets. The clearest architectural precedent remains [Hierarchical Multiscale RNNs (2016/2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.01704): learned boundary detectors control UPDATE, COPY and FLUSH operations without boundary supervision. Its experiments concern language and handwriting, so recommendation gains remain unproven.

Research hypothesis: add a jointly trained boundary gate inside one GRU4Rec network, using current-item embeddings, previous hidden state and optionally observed timestamp gaps to selectively reset memory before the GRU update. Compare against ordinary GRU4Rec and continuous attenuation; monitor gate saturation and reset frequency to detect collapse into always-reset or never-reset behavior. This is a proposed adaptation, not an established result from the cited papers. Resolve the reported final-feature discrepancies first: compare diagnostic and serialized-predictor features and candidate scores on identical histories in evaluation mode; verify padding cannot update recurrent state, identical preprocessing and checkpoint loading, and final-nonpadding readout—never count−1 for left-padded sequences. No discrepancy was diagnosed through this literature search. Keep the boundary mechanism within each category’s single trained network and select using the fixed macro validation HR@10.
